## 2. Why C and R sit well below V: the cascade operating point

With `--cascade`, C is run first and the loss it fitted to its SPICE `.ac` data (the RG-58 figure that was put into the netlist) is handed to R. The fitted loss (32.000005 dB/us) recovers the value that was typed into the netlist (32.0 dB/us; fit residual max |dH| = 1.3e-13), because the LTRA line and the closed-form fit are the same RLC line; so the cascade demonstrates plumbing and provenance, not independent information. The SPICE `tap_H` samples are not used by R. Both tiers therefore run at that loss with **no repeaters**, which the plan itself calls not buildable. R's own default (5 dB/us) is not the headline when `--cascade` is on. Both tiers carry a `loss_db_per_us` sweep, so the same tiers at lower loss are in the data:

| accuracy at loss (dB/us) -> | 0 | 5 | 14 | 32 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| C, mode `layer` (tier default: one ideal gain trim per layer) | 0.863 | 0.827 | 0.751 | 0.663 |
| C, mode `none` (no compensation) | 0.863 | 0.860 | 0.850 | 0.804 |
| C, mode `tap` (ideal per-tap repeater) | 0.863 | 0.860 | 0.852 | 0.805 |
| R (one gain per layer, long taps droop) | 0.861 | 0.845 | 0.789 | 0.701 |

C's per-layer gain trim at the fitted loss (what the single trim per layer has to supply): 1.13, 1.51, 2.85 (linear).

R's required amplifier gain per layer at the run's operating point (dB): L0=22.6, L1=36.3, L2=41.6.

Fitted line loss that `--cascade` hands to R: 32.00 dB/us at 100 MHz.

Two things follow, and they must be kept apart. (1) At 0 dB/us C and R return to (or near) V's accuracy, so the tiers are not broken, and the 32 dB/us, no-repeater operating point is one the plan itself calls not buildable. (2) **Most of C's gap is not line loss but a modelling choice**: C's default compensation (`layer`: one ideal gain trim per layer) scores far lower at the cascade loss than leaving the loss uncompensated (`none`) or using ideal per-tap repeaters (`tap`). `params/circuit_diagnostics.json` holds those two alternative modes; they come from the calibrated behavioural model, not from SPICE, and the C tier's headline was left at the default `layer` mode (the published numbers are as measured). Whether `layer` or `none` is the more faithful model of a real build is not decided by these runs.

**How much of C's gap is line loss?** At the cascade loss C scores 0.663 with its default `layer` mode, 0.804 with `none` (no compensation at all) and 0.805 with `tap` (ideal per-tap repeaters), against V's 0.863. Of C's 20.0-point gap to V, 14.2 points belong to the choice of compensation mode and 5.8 points to the line loss itself (mode `none`). Ideal per-tap repeaters change C's accuracy by +0.1 points relative to doing nothing. Both statements belong with the headline: the cascade operating point is not buildable without repeaters, **and** the default compensation mode over-drives layer 3.

**Why: measured saturation of the tanh inputs** (`scripts/saturation_check.py`, the tiers' own forward code, read-only, first 400 test examples; saturated = |tanh| > 0.95; layer 3 on all 4000 examples in brackets; results in `docs/saturation_check_w32_n400.json`):

| model | layer 1 | layer 2 | layer 3 | accuracy (400) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| V (ideal) | 0.522 | 0.796 | 0.495 (0.499) | 0.863 |
| C, mode `layer` (tier default) | 0.512 | 0.792 | 0.724 (0.728) | 0.657 |
| C, mode `none` | 0.467 | 0.686 | 0.307 (0.311) | 0.762 |
| C, mode `tap` (ideal per-tap repeaters) | 0.508 | 0.782 | 0.498 (0.501) | 0.790 |
| R, `--cascade` (tier default gain rule) | 0.533 | 0.828 | 0.713 (0.717) | 0.675 |
| R, `--cascade` with `tap_equalize` | 0.533 | 0.822 | 0.613 (0.617) | 0.800 |
| R, standalone defaults (5 dB/us) | 0.525 | 0.803 | 0.544 (0.549) | 0.848 |

In layer 3 the tap main cursors run from 1 (no line) to about -35 dB, so the single per-layer trim (here 2.85 in layer 3, 1.13 and 1.51 in layers 1 and 2) also multiplies the almost unattenuated short taps and pushes layer 3 into saturation, well above V's own level; `tap` restores V's level. R's per-layer gain rule shows the same layer-3 saturation at the cascade loss, and R's own per-tap equaliser (optimistic: no repeater noise) raises its accuracy there; that R's rule is a modelling artefact was not shown and is not claimed. Details: `docs/circuit_extraction.md`, "Where C's gap comes from".

Source: `models/train_report.json` (width 8) and `models/train_report_w32.json` (width 32), test set of 4000. The width-8 ternary net, which is the topology the plan specified, **misses the plan's 85 % target at SNR >= 10 dB and collapses the 8PSK class**; the width-32 ternary net recovers it only partly (per-class row above) and also stays below its float counterpart. QPSK gets worse at width 32 (ternary recall below the width-8 ternary net's), and the QPSK / 8PSK pair is the main residual error of the headline model (see V's confusion matrix, figure 6). Both models are reported; neither is hidden.

## 6. What the circuit tier did and did not compute

| quantity | value |
|---|---|
| ngspice version | 42 |
| extraction source | ngspice |
| diff-pair `.dc` tanh fit R^2 | 0.99999997 |
| diff-pair fitted V_sat (mV) | 52.02 |
| fitted line loss at 100 MHz (dB/us) | 32.000 |
| unit-cell `.tran`: examples | 16 |
| unit-cell layer-1 NMSE vs V (variance-normalised, with gain trim) | 0.0220 |
| same, energy-normalised | 0.0187 |
| same cell without gain trim | 0.0267 |
| calibrated behavioural layer 1 vs the SPICE traces (NMSE) | 2.7e-07 |
| RC pool (tau = N*Ts) vs the uniform mean the model was trained with (NMSE) | 0.2156 |
| SPICE wall time of the 16-example unit cell (s) | 20.4 |

What this validates: that the closed-form behavioural line + tanh fit reproduce the SPICE layer-1 traces. What it does not: layers 2-3 use the same line model extrapolated to delays of up to 1.12 microseconds, **never simulated in SPICE**. ngspice's LTRA line has constant R and G = 0, so low-frequency loss is overstated and the tap delay carries an excess group-delay error (`taps.delay_error_s` in `params/circuit_extracted.json`).

| layer 3 | [64, 32, 32] | 65536 | 0 | 2048 | 0 |
| **all layers** |  | 202752 | 0 |  |  |

RTL tool: iverilog 12.0; 64 test examples, first 32 of 128 time steps per example (causal, so the prefix is exact), ADC 8 bits; tier status `ok`.

Limit of a prefix check: with only 32 of 128 steps, the layer-3 taps at lags 32, 48, 64, 80, 96, 112 (k = 2..7) only ever see the zero history, so 6 of the 8 layer-3 tap positions are never driven with data in this run, and the pooled sums are 32-step prefix pools, not the classification pools. The prefix argument (causality) is exact for the steps compared; the long-tap logic is exercised by the width-8 full-length run below.

The 8/8 row is the card as designed, which contains a Python-computed list of material divergences. With the list, Qwen attributes 5/5 injected cards (loose rule; 2/5 under the strict most-severe-metric rule) and gets 3/3 controls right. **Without** the list it attributes **0/5 injected cards** and gets 1/3 controls right; the 1/8 in the table's first column is a control with no divergence, not a found divergent tier. The other controls are false alarms (the summary claims a divergence where there is none). It restates what the card says and does not discover which tier diverges. BitNet's 3/8 is likewise the 3 controls only, reached by writing almost nothing, with 0/5 injected cards attributed (output degenerate here, `docs/llm_eval.md`).
